extracted.intended_audience: scientists and contributors to Nature (authors of letters, book reviewers, textbook writers, and researchers in crystallography)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and informal standards for contributors to a scientific journal (Nature): how to prepare correspondence and reviews, expectations for book/textbook authors, and methodological principles for crystallographic structural analysis. Also useful to researchers preparing observational reports or structural papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial submission policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Editor does not hold himself responsible for opinions expressed by his correspondents. Neither can he undertake to return, or to correspond with the writers of, rejected manuscripts intended for this or any other part of NATURE. No notice is taken of anonymous communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions should be signed (not anonymous). Authors/contributors should not expect returned manuscripts or correspondence about rejected submissions. Opinions published are the contributors' responsibility, not the Editor's.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textbook originality requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: In a subject so new as genetics, something more than an exposition of easily accessible records should be demanded from a considerable text-book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textbook authors should attempt novel presentation or analysis, draw upon related literatures (e.g., horticulture, animal breeding) for illustrative material and suggestive extensions, and offer new themes of discussion even without original discoveries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flag speculative interpretations and need for verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Some interpretations given as accepted doctrine are highly speculative, and some statements of fact are greatly in need of verification. Reports (for example of mutations produced as a direct consequence of changed conditions) should not be accepted without a warning that, until experiments have been repeated on an ample scale and confirmation obtained, evidence of this class has only suggestive value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should explicitly warn readers when interpretations are speculative or based on limited evidence; editors/reviewers/readers should treat unreplicated or preliminary experimental reports as suggestive rather than confirmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include translations and commentary for non-English material
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproduced correspondence in foreign languages would be improved by the addition of English translations and by further comments upon them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing letters, historical correspondence, or primary-source material in other languages, provide translations and editorial commentary to aid readers and contextualize content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biographical/memorial record content standards
rubrics_metrics.description: A roll of service entry should give a brief account of the career, including details of parentage, education, military history, distinctions, and particulars of death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compilations of service/memorial records should be well-arranged, comprehensively produced, and include standard fields for each individual to serve as an adequate record and memorial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance and intelligibility of collected essays
rubrics_metrics.description: Essays on recent achievements should be written so as to be intelligible to readers whose special knowledge is not profound, while still being of interest to advanced researchers; avoid an unbalanced mix of general-interest articles and very specialised topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors of collected volumes should aim for articles that are accessible to educated non-specialists yet valuable to practitioners; curate contents to avoid over-representation of wartime- or niche-specific topics that may age quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational report standards (instrumentation and conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting observational work (e.g., polarisation of diffused light under the sea), provide details of detector/apparatus, measuring principle, observation depth and conditions (clarity, sky state), and note whether repeated observations produced consistent results; report apparent uncertainties or doubtful differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include apparatus design, environmental conditions, repetition status, and candid statements about the degree of confidence in any small effects or doubtful findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of X-rays and crystals to probe atomic structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern advances come from combining X-rays and crystals: crystals as repeated atomic patterns amplify atomic properties so that X-ray methods can examine atomic arrangements and infer material properties from unit-cell information and reflection intensities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural studies should exploit the complementarity of X-ray diffraction and crystalline symmetry to determine unit cell dimensions, molecule counts per cell, and relative distributions in the cell as a foundation for structural hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply crystallographic symmetry and ionic models to predict structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Crystallographic symmetry, supplemented by understanding of ionic character (grouping of positive ions around negatives and vice versa), can permit prediction of probable crystal forms (e.g., rock-salt, fluorspar, ice) which X-ray data can then verify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use chemical charge considerations and symmetry constraints to generate plausible structural models before (or alongside) detailed analysis of X-ray intensities; this can make analysis tractable for many inorganic crystals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of radius of combination (isomorphous substitution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distances between centers of neighboring atoms often change predictably when substitutions are made in isomorphous compounds; one may treat an atom's 'radius of combination' as approximately constant within the substitution range to aid analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use systematic substitution series (F→Cl→Br→I, etc.) and measured distance changes to infer characteristic combination radii for elements; but avoid overinterpreting a strict, invariant atomic radius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and choose appropriate bonding models
rubrics_metrics.description: Different crystals exhibit different bond characters: strong electron-sharing (covalent) bonds (diamond), ionic bonds (rocksalt, fluorspar), and weak residual forces between discrete molecules (organic crystals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a structural model consistent with expected bonding type: treat atoms as centers in ionic lattices, consider electron-sharing networks for covalent solids, and model molecular packing and weak intermolecular forces for organic crystals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplement X-ray evidence with chemical/molecular hypotheses for organic crystals
rubrics_metrics.description: Because organic crystals are complex, X-ray intensities and cell dimensions alone may be insufficient; one should test chemical hypotheses about molecular size and shape (e.g., benzene rings) to see if such molecules can be fitted consistently into the known unit cells.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate plausible molecular shapes from chemical knowledge, then check for geometric fit with measured unit-cell parameters and relative molecule placements; a good fit strengthens the structural hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative structural transformations to inform hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparisons between known structures (e.g., diamond → graphite transformations, sheet separations) can suggest plausible routes to other structures (e.g., ring structures), guiding hypotheses about molecular arrangements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use known structural relations and plausible transformations as heuristic tools to generate models for complex or derived structures; corroborate with experimental data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relate anisotropic thermal expansion and cleavage to bond nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in expansion coefficients and cleavage behavior (e.g., bismuth expansion along axis vs across; diamond's small expansion; graphite's large axial expansion) are connected to the nature and directionality of bonds in the crystal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret mechanical/thermal anisotropies as diagnostic of bond strengths and directions; use such macroscopic measurements to infer bonding character and inform structural models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report limitations of analogy between optical and molecular problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogies between light reflection/transmission and molecular passage (e.g., funnels) can mislead: molecular problems may be dominated by collisions and statistics over mean free paths rather than simple geometric optics rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing by analogy, explicitly state and check the assumptions (e.g., mean free path relative to aperture size, role of collisions). Define measurement tolerances (elements of area) and ensure probabilistic/kinetic factors are properly included.
